Minor thing - watch the em dashes in paragraphs three and four, house style is plain hyphens.

The closing ask is also broad to the point of being generic; narrowing it would signal more conviction, not less.

Where it goes soft is on the quality issue: "The financial impact is small (approximately EUR 3 million in returns and rework) but the customer has placed HPC on enhanced quality monitoring for 12 months" understates what enhanced monitoring actually means for wallet share and new program awards, and we should say so rather than let the EUR 3 million number do the reassuring. The procurement update is also thinner than it should be - "EUR 2.1 million of annualised savings, against a year-one target of EUR 5 million" invites the obvious question of whether the remaining 2.9 is identified, in diligence, or still to be found, and the draft doesn't answer. Lehmann gets a single sentence with no commentary on early read, which feels like a miss given commercial is one of the three value creation levers. drafts.note: The letter reads cleanly and the thesis comes through quickly - the three pillars framing works, and the ARR trajectory from EUR 28m to EUR 38m gives readers something concrete to latch onto. Where it gets thin is the proof behind the claims. "Independent customer research rates the Company significantly higher than the principal Nordic competitor Yardi Nordic on usability and feature completeness" is doing a lot of work without naming the source or giving a number, and the same goes for the "approximately 40%" legacy penetration figure. The returns bridge is also weaker than it should be - we tell LPs ARR goes to EUR 95m and that this produces 2.8x and 23% IRR, but nothing on exit multiple assumption, leverage, or margin trajectory, and I think sophisticated readers will notice. One small housekeeping point: 240'000 should be 240,000 for an English-language investor letter. Finally, the closing paragraph is a bit boilerplate - "defensible competitive position in a growing category and a credible operational team" could describe almost any deal, so consider something more specific to Nordic SaaS.

drafts.note: The letter has a clear spine and the big news lands where it should - NorTech leading, two challenges acknowledged honestly, then ESG and forward look. The Eltex passage is the strongest paragraph in the draft; the backlog growth from EUR 285 million to EUR 480 million does real work and I'd protect it. The Continental Plastics and Drift sections are also well-pitched - specific, unflinching, and paired with concrete responses, which is the tone LPs want on bad news. Watch the house style throughout: you've written "19.7 percent", "3 percent", "40 percent" and so on where we use the % symbol. The second paragraph is also doing too much - Helvetia, Lumen, Brightway and Eltex are crammed into a single run-on sentence held together by semicolons, and Brightway in particular deserves its own beat rather than being a way-station between the new acquisitions and the Eltex highlight. One small logical snag worth a look: you say "across the remaining eight active portfolio companies" and later "all eight active portfolio companies have completed or are in the final stages of SBTi submission", but only six are named - either the reader should be told there are two you're not discussing, or the number needs reconciling. Finally, "the recently-acquired Lumen Specialty Chemicals" is vague next to the precise acquisition dates you give for Helvetia and Continental; give it a month.

The LP base detail ("92 institutional investors across 26 countries") lands well and the strategy paragraph gives enough shape to be useful without overclaiming. Two things to fix before it goes out. First, house style: "96 percent" should be "96%", and check that no em dashes have slipped in elsewhere in the file. Second, the middle paragraph is doing too much work in one breath - the sentence beginning "Re-up rates from existing LPs were strong at 96 percent by capital, and the Fund welcomed new investors across three of the largest US public pension funds, two Asian sovereign wealth funds, and a number of European and North American family offices and endowments" would read better split in two. Also worth a sanity check on "three of the largest US public pension funds" - that phrasing is vague enough to invite questions, and you may want either to name them (with permission) or soften to "several large US public pension funds". Strategy section is fine but "Our investment team has been preparing Fund V's pipeline for many months" is filler - either cut it or say something concrete about pipeline visibility.
